newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala's ex-rebels face uncertain future.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala's ex-rebels face uncertain future.

text.p: Ex-guerrillas on Friday entered U.N.-monitored disarmament camps for a two-month period prior to their return to civilian life, but they said their future in post-war Guatemala was far from clear.

Several former rebels were counting on the government to buy them land for cooperatives after they abandoned the shifting mountain hideouts where they have lived during more than three decades of civil war. But the issue appeared to remain unsettled.

"Sincerely, we haven't spoken about land in any of our meetings yet," Alvaro Colom, a government member of a commission to design programmes to help former rebels return to civilian life, told reporters on Friday.

Colom and other government officials were attending a ceremony at Camp Claudia, 48 miles (77 km) south of Guatemala City, one of eight disarmament camps officially turned over to a few thousand rebels on Friday.

An estimated 140,000 people, mostly civilians, were killed or disappeared during Guatemala's civil war, the longest in Central America and the last to finish. The war officially ended with a peace accord on Dec. 29 between the government and leftist rebels of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG).
Under terms of the accord, guerrillas will spend two months in the camps and turn in weapons under international scrutiny. During this time they will live in plastic and metal barracks.
Beginning on Monday a mission of unarmed U.N. observers posted next to each camp will register guerrillas living there. Two months later, they must all be gone.
"I don't have any idea where I'll go. It hasn't been decided where the government will buy land for us," said ex-rebel Guillermo Figueroa, who fought under the name Lieutenant Raul.

Figueroa, who has lost track of his family and would like to live in a community with other ex-combatants, is training to be a bodyguard for former URNG commanders. He said people from his front of the URNG wanted to learn such diverse careers as nursing, animal husbandry, carpentry and sewing.

David Stephen, outgoing director of the United Nations Mission for Human Rights Verification in Guatemala, said the ex-guerrillas must leave the camps by May 3. "Our aim is to get everyone out of the camps and into ... training courses and programmes to allow them to reintegrate themselves into society."

But Stephen acknowledged that in other countries it has not always been easy to reintegrate ex-rebels into society. "Among the URNG here there are certainly people who have been fighting in very difficult terrain for 10-15 or even more years so they will need counselling to get back into civil society," he said.

Jorge Soto, formerly known as guerrilla commander Pablo Monsanto, warned that demobilization should not be arbitrary and urged the United Nations not to force the guerrillas after May 3 "out on the street without a roof over their heads."

Soto said polls of rank-and-file have shown that, like Figueroa, a majority of the ex-guerrillas want to live together in small cooperatives or communities. The government should fund land purchases using international aid promised to help Guatemala's peace process, he said.
